title: Motor finance legal challenge to be heard in February 2027
source_summary: The Upper Tribunal has confirmed it will hear the legal challenges to our motor finance compensation scheme between 16 to 26 February 2027. The scheme was challenged by 3 lenders - Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services, and Crédit Agricole Auto Finance - and by Consumer Voice, represented by Courmacs Legal. The scheme is currently partially suspended. However, firms must keep preparing for the scheme and progress complaints as far as possible.Our scheme is the quickest, fairest and most efficient way to compensate consumers and we will defend it robustly.Advice for lenders Lenders must comply with the scheme rules that remain in force. This includes sending letters to some consumers not owed compensation under the scheme.Firms should plan for the possibility that, if the scheme or parts of it are quashed, there may be no motor finance compensation scheme and no complaint handling pause. In that scenario, lenders would need to be operationally and financially ready to resolve complaints through the usual complaint-handling process and within the usual statutory timescales.We expect lenders to plan rigorously for this scenario, make the necessary financial provisions and engage with their auditors.We encourage firms to contact us if they have questions. We will keep our firm web page updated with the latest information.

source_name: fca_rss
title: Two plead guilty after clients lose £2m in fraud case
source_summary: Two people who worked at financial advice firms have pleaded guilty to fraud after 4 clients lost £2m. Kerry Nelson, the director of Nexus Independent Financial Advisers Limited and Nexus Investment Managers Limited, and Jacqueline Stephens, the firms' business operations manager, admitted all charges brought by the FCA at Portsmouth Crown Court.They admitted defrauding clients between January 2019 and January 2023 and using false documents as part of the fraud. Nelson has also admitted a money laundering offence after money was withdrawn from the firms, which she used to fund her extravagant lifestyle.Therese Chambers, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:'This was a serious breach of trust. Nelson and Stephens caused significant losses to clients who relied on them. We will continue to act where people exploit clients for their own gain.'Nelson and Stephens will be sentenced at Portsmouth Crown Court on 10 December 2026. The FCA will seek confiscation proceedings to deprive Kerry Nelson of any financial benefit from her criminal conduct.Notes to editorsThe FCA started criminal proceedings against Kerry Nelson and Jacqueline Stephens in February 2025. For more details see, FCA charges two individuals with multiple fraud charges. They pleaded guilty at Portsmouth Crown Court on 12 October 2026.Fraud by abuse of position is an offence under sections 1 and 4 of the Fraud Act 2006.Using a false instrument is an offence under section 3 of the Forgery and Counterfeiting Act 1981.Converting or transferring criminal property is an offence under section 327(1) of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002.Confiscation proceedings will be pursued under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002.Nexus IFA and Nexus IM were authorised by the FCA. Nexus IFA had permissions to provide investment, mortgage and pension advice and Nexus IM to provide discretionary fund management services. Neither firm was permitted to hold or control client money.On 25 January 2023, the FCA imposed restrictions preventing both firms from carrying on regulated activity and from reducing the value of the assets they held. The High Court placed both firms into administration on 26 January 2023.

source_name: fca_rss
title: Three arrests in major FCA operation against criminal insider dealing ring
source_summary: The FCA has conducted a major operation to disrupt a suspected organised criminal group for engaging in insider dealing and money laundering. On 13 October, 3 individuals were arrested following a joint operation by the FCA and the National Crime Agency (NCA). More than 100 FCA and NCA staff took part in searches at 5 residential premises in London and Manchester.More than 30 mobile phones, laptops and tablets were seized in searches conducted by FCA investigators.All 3 suspects are in the process of being interviewed by the FCA at police stations in London and Manchester.Steve Smart, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:'Insider dealing is a serious threat to the integrity of our markets. Working with partners, we will continue to use all the powers at our disposal to crack down on serious and organised crime groups engaged in market abuse.'In 2025/26, the FCA secured 4 insider dealing convictions, with 2 resulting in record sentences totalling 11 years of imprisonment. Twelve people were fined a total of £1.77m for insider dealing, market manipulation and making misleading statements.Notes to editorsThe FCA cannot comment further at this time but will provide more details when appropriate.Fighting financial crime is a priority in the FCA’s 5-year strategy.If you have information concerning insider dealing you can contact the FCA by phone on 0800 111 6768 or by using the FCA’s reporting form. Information can be passed confidentially.The FCA enables a fair and thriving financial services market for the good of consumers and the economy. Find out more about the FCA.

title: Liam Coleman appointed as chair of the Financial Ombudsman Service
source_summary: The FCA Board has appointed Liam Coleman as chair of the Financial Ombudsman Service, with the approval of the Treasury. Liam will take up the permanent role on 10 October 2026 for a 3-year term, having served as interim chair for the last year.Ashley Alder, chair of the FCA, commented: 'Liam has brought strong leadership and valuable insight to the Financial Ombudsman Service over the past year. His extensive experience across financial services, regulation and public service organisations will be invaluable as we work together to support a redress system that is fair, predictable and effective for consumers and firms.'Commenting on the appointment, Mr Coleman said: 'I am honoured to take on the permanent role as chair of the Financial Ombudsman Service. It plays a vital role in upholding fairness and trust in the financial system. I am pleased to be able to continue to work with the rest of the Board, the executive team, and our wider stakeholders.'Liam is also group chair of London & Quadrant Housing Trust. He has extensive financial services and public-sector experience, including previous roles at the FCA, NHS Foundation Trust, Nationwide Building Society, Royal Bank of Scotland and Cooperative Bank.Notes to editorsThe FCA is required by the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA) to appoint the chair of the Financial Ombudsman Service, with the appointment being approved by the Treasury.The Board of the Financial Ombudsman Service is responsible for ensuring that the service is properly resourced and able to carry out its work effectively and independently.The Financial Ombudsman Service was set up to resolve complaints between financial businesses and their customers. It can help with most financial services – including banking, insurance, loans, mortgages, pensions and investments. From 1 April 2019, its remit was extended to cover complaints from larger small and medium sized businesses and about claims management companies.The FCA and the Financial Ombudsman Service are working with the government to transform the UK’s redress system and the way in which the Ombudsman operates within it to deliver a service that is consistent, predictable and fair for both firms and consumers, now and in the future.Find out more information about the FCA.Find out more information about the Financial Ombudsman Service.

source_name: fca_rss
title: Strong compliance functions support trusted corporate finance markets
source_summary: Corporate finance firms help businesses raise funding and implement strategic transactions, supporting investment and growth.This brings responsibility: clients need to be able to trust that firms will act with integrity and manage any conflicts of interest. That trust underpins effective wholesale markets activity.In our Regulatory Priorities Report, we said we would assess corporate finance firms’ compliance functions and their ability to challenge the business effectively. We surveyed 411 corporate finance firms about their compliance resources and activities, receiving 382 responses. Although most firms reported carrying out key compliance activities, the findings also show where more needs to be done.There is no single blueprint for what effective compliance looks like. We found that firms operate a range of different practices. But the findings also underline an overarching principle that compliance cannot be seen as simply a series of tasks, but a culture that senior managers must embed throughout the business.

source_name: fca_rss
title: New rules to make long-term investment funds clearer
source_summary: The FCA has set out clearer expectations for asset managers about long-term investments, such as property. This will help give the market more confidence to invest in funds that support private markets.The new rules mean that investors will have to give 90 days' notice to access their funds but will be more certain that they will receive their money.For investors, this means the fund should be clearer from the start about how quickly they can get their money back and whether the fund is right for their needs.Currently some of these funds allow people to take money out daily with no notice period. During periods of stress or volatility there is a risk that some funds may suspend all payments due to lack of available cash. Some are also holding extra cash, leaving less invested in their intended assets.Rushed sales can lower prices, harm investors who stay invested and put pressure on markets.The new notice period would give managers time to sell assets in an orderly way and make liquidity-driven suspensions less likely.Existing funds would have 2 years to comply and give investors at least 1 year’s notice.The proposals bring the UK into line with new international liquidity standards for open ended funds.Michelle Beck, director, markets, at the FCA, said: 'Funds should be clear about whether they offer quick access or are built for longer-term investments like property. Our rules will help firms make that clearer and give the market more confidence to invest.'Notes to editorsRead CP26/35: Fair redemption terms for authorised funds investing in illiquid assets.The FCA is asking for feedback on the proposals by 11 December 2026.The consultation covers authorised fund managers of non-UCITS retail schemes, known as NURS.The FCA uses the term 'inherently illiquid assets' for assets that cannot normally be sold quickly without a significant loss in value. These can include property and infrastructure investments.Fund managers could set a notice period longer than the minimum where the fund’s assets or investment strategy require it.
